name: Mandate — the send gate and approval record for AI in independent insurance agencies
one_liner: For principals of 5–50 person independent P&C insurance agencies, Mandate sits between every AI tool the staff already use (ChatGPT drafts, EZLynx EVA, AI texting, voice receptionists) and the client, holding each outbound message in one approval queue with a coverage-risk flag and an immutable, exportable E&O record of who approved what.
problem: Independent agencies went from 15% AI use in 2024 to 46% in 2026 (Big "I" Agency Universe Study), but only ~8% have AI embedded in daily workflow and only ~13% have any written AI policy; the top two named concerns in the Big "I"/ACT survey are data-privacy/compliance risk (24%) and inaccurate outputs (22%). Meanwhile the classic E&O claim against an agency is a communication failure: the client says "I asked you to add the trailer / you said I was covered", and the agency cannot prove what was said, by whom, and when. Today AI output is scattered: a CSR pastes ChatGPT text into Outlook, EVA drafts an email inside EZLynx, an AI texting tool answers an ID-card request, a voice receptionist promises a callback. Each lives in a different log, or no log. The principal's only control is trust. The workaround today is either banning AI (losing the speed) or policing it with spot checks of the AMS activity log after the fact, which proves nothing about the draft that went out at 4:58pm on a Friday.
target_customer: The agency principal or operations/compliance lead at a 5–50 employee independent P&C agency (US; ~37,000 independent agencies per the 2026 Agency Universe Study). They own the E&O policy and the tech budget; published benchmarks put client-experience software spend at roughly $18k–$45k/yr for an average agency, so a $300–$900/month line is in range. Secondary buyer: the agency network/cluster or E&O carrier who would push it to member agencies.
why_now: Three things changed inside twelve months: AI use in agencies tripled (46% in 2026 vs 15% in 2024) while formal AI policy stayed at ~13%; AMS vendors shipped AI that drafts and in some cases auto-replies (EZLynx EVA drafts, automated text replies for ID cards); and the infrastructure pattern for this exists publicly — DigitalOcean's Action Gateway (Oct 2026) makes "a model's tool call is a request, not authority: allow, deny, or ask a human" a shipped, named product pattern for developers. Nobody has packaged that pattern for a non-technical regulated SMB where the "tool call" is an email to a policyholder.
comparables: Covera (YC F26, covera-agents.com) — AI workflows for independent P&C agencies (submissions, ACORD prep, carrier-portal quoting) with staff review and an E&O activity trail; it is the doer, not a neutral gate, and its record only covers work Covera itself did. Gap: it cannot govern ChatGPT, the texting tool, or the voice receptionist. Trussed AI (trussed.ai) — AI governance control plane sold to regulated enterprises, runtime policy + audit; built for an enterprise CISO, not a 12-person agency with no IT staff. Smarsh — communications supervision and archiving for financial services including brokers; archives and surveils after the fact, enterprise priced, not a pre-send gate. Magellan (Bridge Insure + Rhodian) — agency AI communications platform with compliance monitoring; monitoring, not a hard send gate, and bundled with its own comms stack. Microsoft Agent 365 ($15/user/mo) and Purview ($12/user/mo) — real governance but only inside Microsoft, and they govern agents, not the CSR who pasted ChatGPT output into Outlook. OfficeAgent ($149–$399/mo) proves the approval-before-send pattern sells at SMB prices, but in property management. The gap: a cheap, cross-tool, hard send gate plus exportable E&O evidence pack, sold to the agency principal rather than to IT.
market_note: Estimate, stated as such: ~37,000 US independent agencies (2026 Agency Universe Study); they place ~62% of US P&C premium and 87.7% of commercial lines. If 10% of agencies buy at $500/month average, that is roughly $22M ARR — small but real, and the natural expansion is per-seat pricing, the agency networks/clusters (which buy for hundreds of members at once) and E&O carriers who could fund or discount it. Willingness to pay is anchored on E&O deductibles (typically five figures) and on the $18k–$45k/yr these agencies already spend on client-experience software. Not a venture-scale market on agencies alone; the thesis is that the same gate resells into mortgage brokers, RIAs, title and property management, each with its own evidence export.
risks: Distribution: 37,000 small agencies is a slow, conference-and-cluster sale with no viral loop; CAC could swamp a $500/month ACV unless a network or E&O carrier channel works. Displacement: Applied/Vertafore/EZLynx can bolt an approval queue onto the AMS the agency already pays for, and "it's in the AMS" beats "it's another vendor"; our defence is being the only neutral gate over tools the AMS does not own. Trust and liability: sitting in the send path of a regulated business means an outage stops client email, and the evidence record has to survive a deposition — both raise the bar on engineering and insurance well above a normal SaaS v1.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) Principals will accept friction on outbound client messages — if approval adds 20 seconds per email, CSRs route around it and the gate becomes shelfware; the product has to auto-approve the boring 80% (ID cards, scheduling, acknowledgements) and only stop coverage, pricing, cancellation and claims language. 2) We can technically intercept before send across the actual stack — Microsoft 365/Google transport rules and the texting vendor's webhook must let us hold a message; if EZLynx or a voice agent sends out-of-band, our record has holes and the E&O value collapses. 3) The buyer feels this as pain today rather than after their first AI-caused claim — 46% adoption with 13% policy coverage suggests the gap is real, but "we'll write a policy memo" is the cheap substitute we actually compete with.
first_customers: Ten principals of 5–50 person P&C agencies reachable this month: (1) Big "I" state association meetings and the ACT (Agents Council for Technology) work groups, where the 2026 tech survey respondents live; (2) the r/InsuranceAgent and Insurance Agency Owners / "Agency Growth" Facebook and LinkedIn groups where AI-tool threads run weekly; (3) attendees/exhibitor lists of ITC Vegas and Big "I" Legislative Conference; (4) agency networks and clusters (SIAA, Smart Choice, Renaissance) whose member-services teams broker vendors to hundreds of small agencies; (5) E&O program managers at Swiss Re/Westport and Utica, who publish the loss-prevention guidance that already tells agencies to document every coverage conversation.
validation_test: This week: offer 10 agency principals a free "AI exposure audit" — they forward or grant read-only access to one week of outbound client email and text from the three accounts where AI is used; we return a one-page report listing every message that contained coverage, pricing, binding or claims language with no recorded human approver, plus a sample evidence pack for one message. Pass: 6 of 10 agree to the audit, and at least 3 ask "can you make this stop before it goes out?" or accept a paid pilot at $500/month. Fail: principals shrug at the report or say their AMS log is enough.
build_plan: Narrowest first version: one agency, one channel. (1) Microsoft 365 transport rule routes outbound mail from the agency's shared service@ and the CSR mailboxes through Mandate; (2) a classifier (GPT-class model, cheap) tags each message as routine (ID card, scheduling, acknowledgement, document request) or risky (coverage statement, premium/quote figure, cancellation/non-renewal, claim advice, binding language) — routine releases instantly, risky holds; (3) a mobile-first approval queue for the principal/licensed reviewer: approve, edit-and-approve, or kill, with a 10-minute SLA timer and auto-escalation; (4) every message, whether held or released, is written to an append-only record with the draft, the source (which human or which AI tool), the edits, the approver, the timestamp and the final sent copy; (5) one button: "Export E&O evidence pack for this client" — a dated PDF + CSV bundle for a specific policyholder. Cut for v1: SMS and voice, AMS write-back, policy builder UI, SOC 2, multi-tenant admin. Add SMS second (it is where the auto-replies live), AMS write-back third.
reasoning:
Mandate wins the venture track because its failure mode is the one I can most plausibly design around. The strongest reason it dies is friction: if a principal has to approve every email, staff route around the gate. The narrow first version answers that directly — auto-release the routine 80% (ID cards, scheduling, documents) and only hold five named categories of language (coverage, pricing, binding, cancellation, claims advice). That makes it a product you can pilot in one agency in weeks. The research also found a genuine gap rather than an empty field: Covera (YC F26) does agency AI work with a review step but is the doer, not a neutral gate over ChatGPT and the texting bot; Trussed and Smarsh solve this for enterprises and CISOs, not 12-person agencies; Microsoft Agent 365 governs agents inside Microsoft, not the CSR pasting model output into Outlook. And the numbers back the timing: agency AI use tripled to 46% in 2026 while only ~13% have any AI policy, with inaccurate outputs and compliance named as the top two concerns. I scored timing 8 (a measured one-year change plus the Action Gateway pattern shipping in October) and held pain, market pull, gap and wedge at 7 because I verified competitors and spend benchmarks but have not spoken to a principal; nothing here earns a 9. Verdict is watch, not dig_deeper, because the distribution story (37,000 small agencies, conference-and-cluster selling) is the unresolved part.

It builds on Holdroom and Receipts from the library but is not a repeat: Holdroom supervises live AI phone calls for ops teams, Receipts records payer-portal submissions for medical billers; Mandate's buyer is the insurance agency principal and the workflow is pre-send interception of written client communications across tools the agency does not own. Different buyer, different channel, different artifact.

Figures runs the other track and shares nothing with Mandate — different audience (designers and makers vs agency principals), different problem (public data nobody has presented well vs regulated communication risk), different bookmarks (the RWE-Bench physical-engineering post and the interface-grammar post, vs the Action Gateway and multi-agent-attribution posts). Its pain is latent: nobody asks for a patent-drawing browser. What makes people notice it is the first screenshot of the wall — that is the entire launch strategy, and it is why shareability and wow score 8 while usefulness sits at 6. Freshness is only 6 honestly: DeepPatent has been public since 2022, so what is new is the cheapness of browser-side semantic search, not the dataset. could_grow is true — a visual prior-art pass for design patents is something IP paralegals would pay for — but as a weekend build it is a gallery, not a business.

Both tracks reached 6, so both are filed. Mandate goes top-level on score; that is placement, not preference.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Mandate — approval gate + E&O evidence record for AI client communications in independent insurance agencies. KEPT: verified a real adoption/governance gap (46% AI use vs 13% with a policy), a named buyer with a budget line, and competitors that each miss the cross-tool pre-send gate.
2. Portal Clerk — deterministic portal-submission robot with human approval and audit for freight brokers / permit filers, inspired by Pomerado. DROPPED: the same buyer and workflow are already contested by Vooma (~$16.6M raised), HappyRobot (~$200M raised, Series C Aug 2026), Drumkit ($1,500/mo pilots) and Skyvern ($29–$149/mo self-serve), and the freight wedge in particular is well funded; no narrow buyer left that a small team reaches first.
3. Agent Attribution Desk — a "who did what" ledger across a person's many personal agents, from @sriramk's post. DROPPED on feasibility, not desire: the Gmail and Calendar user APIs do not expose which OAuth client made a change (actor-app attribution is a Workspace admin audit-log feature), so the core promise cannot be delivered for the consumer/prosumer buyer the post describes.
4. Clinic send-gate (dental/medical front-office version of Mandate). DROPPED as the weaker twin: HIPAA, BAAs and EHR integration make the first version months longer, and Weave/Arini/Assort already own the channel; same idea, harder entry.

BUILD
1. Figures — 350,000 CC0 design-patent drawings as a searchable infinite wall. KEPT: dataset confirmed CC0 and downloadable, search runs client-side so there is no API cost, and no free drawing-first browser exists (Google Patents and Espacenet are text-first; PNNL VIPS is DOE-only).
2. Agent X-ray for any website — paste a URL, see what an AI agent could actually do there. DROPPED: at least five free scanners already do this (AI Agent Readiness Scanner, Frase, Web Specification, agentready, Cloudflare's isitagentready), plus a crowd of free agentic-commerce readiness scanners.
3. MCP capability card — one-screen plain-English list of every action an MCP server exposes, with destructive ones flagged. DROPPED: close prior art in MCP Permission Scanner and mcp-risk, and it serves the same developer audience as the library's existing Shelf and Skillscope.
4. Interface Grammar — turn a screenshot or OpenAPI spec into the nouns and verbs an agent should operate on, from @Mappletons' post. DROPPED: genuinely little prior art, but the output is an abstract diagram rather than something anyone would post, and the input (a design file) is too fiddly for a one-box toy.
5. Genie 4 world-model toy. DROPPED on access: Genie 4 is trusted-tester only, with no public API, no pricing and no general availability — nothing to build on this weekend.
research_notes:
22 tool calls budgeted; 20 used (3 reading, 10 venture, 7 build). I cannot see images, so for the four video-only bookmarks I relied on post text plus Web Summary.

Reading (3): Summarised DigitalOcean's Action Gateway — confirmed the allow/deny/ask-a-human policy model and that it is sold to developer teams, which became the venture's "why now" and its explicit contrast (the same pattern, repackaged for a non-technical regulated SMB). Summarised Pomerado (YC F26) — confirmed it generates deterministic integrations from a described website workflow, which spawned the Portal Clerk candidate. Summarised Genie 4 — the finding that it is trusted-tester only with no public API or pricing killed the world-model build candidate before it cost me any build-pot calls.

Venture (10): Two keyword searches on agent attribution and approval tooling returned mostly SEO filler and were close to wasted. The productive calls were Perplexity summaries that each reshaped the candidate: a scan of agent-governance platforms showed everything is enterprise-priced (Microsoft Agent 365 $15/user/mo, IBM from $3,500/mo) or platform-locked, which pushed me away from a generic governance play; a property-management/insurance approval-workflow summary surfaced OfficeAgent at $149–$399/mo, proving the approve-before-send pattern sells at SMB prices; the Big "I" summary produced the decisive numbers (46% AI use in 2026 vs 15% in 2024, 8% with AI in daily workflow, 13% with a formal AI policy, 24%/22% naming compliance and inaccurate outputs) and named Covera, Trussed, Smarsh, Magellan and FieldWatch; a follow-up on Covera and Trussed established that Covera is a doer with its own review trail rather than a neutral cross-tool gate — that distinction is now the whole wedge. A Gmail/Calendar API check killed the agent-attribution venture on feasibility. Freight and Skyvern summaries (Vooma ~$16.6M, HappyRobot ~$200M and a reported ~$250k minimum, Drumkit $1,500/mo pilot, Skyvern $29–$149/mo with human-in-the-loop gated to Enterprise) closed the portal-automation gap for a solo builder.

Build (7): Checked prior art for the agent-readiness scanner (five free tools found — dropped), the MCP capability card (MCP Permission Scanner and mcp-risk found — dropped), and interface-grammar extraction (little prior art, but weak as a shareable toy). Then three calls on patent imagery: confirmed Google Patents BigQuery does not include drawing images and USPTO ODP has no per-drawing image endpoint (20 downloads per file per key per year), compared paid routes (SerpApi, EPO OPS 4GB/week free, PatentsView keys suspended), and finally confirmed DeepPatent — 350,000+ PNG design-patent drawings with patent IDs, CC0, direct download, plus DeepPatent2 at 2M+ under CC BY 4.0. That last finding is what moved Figures from "needs a paid API, probably too expensive" to buildable in a weekend with zero per-query cost, and is why buildability scored 7 rather than 4. A search for an existing patent-drawing gallery found only research papers (DeepPatent retrieval benchmarks), a DOE-scoped visual search at PNNL, and museum exhibits — no free consumer-facing wall.
prototype_summary: An interactive prototype of Mandate, showing the scattered unprovable AI messaging of a typical insurance agency versus a single approval queue with risk-flagged holds, approver stamps, and an exportable E&O evidence pack.
